Newborn Care

Soothing a Crying Baby and Understanding Colic

Updated: July 1, 2026

Crying is a newborn’s entire vocabulary , hunger, tiredness, discomfort, and "I do not know, I just need you" all come out the same way. Some crying has a fix, some does not, and both are normal. Here is how to soothe, what colic really means, and how to take care of yourself through the loud weeks.

Why babies cry

Run the checklist first: hungry, tired, dirty diaper, too hot or cold, needs a burp, overstimulated, or simply wants to be held. Most crying maps to one of these, and the checklist becomes automatic within weeks.

Crying also tends to increase over the first weeks of life, often peaking around six to eight weeks before easing , a well-documented pattern in healthy babies. More crying at this stage does not mean you are doing something wrong.

Soothing techniques worth trying

Newborns are comforted by womb-like sensations. Try a snug swaddle (arms secure, hips loose, always back-sleeping), rhythmic shushing or steady white noise about as loud as the crying, and gentle swaying or rocking while you hold baby close.

Sucking is powerfully calming too , the breast, a clean finger, or a pacifier once feeding is established. Add motion (a walk, a carrier, a rocking chair) and skin-to-skin contact, and rotate through the options calmly; sometimes the third or fourth try lands.

No technique works every time, and that is not failure. Sometimes the win is a calmer parent holding a still-crying baby , babies borrow our calm.

What colic is , and is not

Colic is commonly described by the rule of threes: crying more than three hours a day, more than three days a week, for at least three weeks, in an otherwise healthy, feeding, growing baby. It often clusters in the evening and starts in the first weeks of life.

Colic is not caused by bad parenting, and a colicky baby is not sick , by definition, colic is intense crying in a healthy baby. It typically fades on its own by around three to four months. That does not make it easy; it makes it survivable.

Coping when the crying wears you down

Prolonged crying is genuinely stressful , your nervous system is built to respond to it. Tag out with a partner or helper before you reach your limit, not after. Even a ten-minute walk outside resets more than you would expect.

If you are alone and overwhelmed, it is safe and okay to place your baby on their back in the crib, walk into another room, and take a few minutes to breathe. A crying baby in a safe crib is fine; a parent past their breaking point is the real risk.

Never shake a baby

No matter how long the crying goes on, never shake a baby. Shaking can cause serious, permanent brain injury or death in seconds. This is exactly why stepping away to calm down is the responsible move, not a shameful one.

If you ever feel close to the edge, put the baby down safely and call someone , a partner, a friend, a family member, or a parent helpline. Needing backup during the colic weeks is universal, not exceptional.

When crying deserves a call to the doctor

Call your pediatrician if the crying sounds different , high-pitched, weak, or moaning , or comes with fever, vomiting, poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, unusual sleepiness, or a baby who cannot be consoled at all for hours.

Also reach out if the crying pattern changes suddenly, or simply if your instincts say something is off. Confirming a baby is healthy is a legitimate reason for a visit, and it changes how the crying feels at home.

Key takeaways

  • Run the basics first: hunger, tiredness, diaper, temperature, burp, overstimulation.
  • Swaddle, shush or white noise, sway, and suck are the classic calming tools.
  • Colic is intense crying in a healthy baby , the rule of threes , and fades by 3–4 months.
  • It is safe to put a crying baby down in the crib and step away to reset; never shake a baby.
  • Different-sounding cries, fever, poor feeding, or inconsolable hours mean call the doctor.

Frequently asked questions

How do I know if my baby has colic?

The common definition is crying more than three hours a day, three or more days a week, for three weeks or longer in a baby who is otherwise healthy, feeding, and growing. Your pediatrician can confirm nothing else is going on , which is worth doing for reassurance alone.

Will responding to every cry spoil my newborn?

No. In the newborn months, responding to crying builds security, not bad habits. Babies this young cannot be spoiled by comfort.

What should I do if I feel angry when my baby will not stop crying?

Frustration is a normal human response to prolonged crying. Place your baby safely on their back in the crib, step into another room, breathe, and call someone for backup. Never shake a baby , stepping away is the safe, responsible choice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
